sections.title: Purpose — Improvement · Maintenance
sections.html:
10.1 · Purpose

Purpose — Improvement · Maintenance

◈ Improving

Through measurement and record-keeping, establish what is better as data, and raise profiles and recipes step by step. Improvement accumulates only on comparable records, not on instinct.

◈ Maintaining

Reproduce a quality already reached even as the batch, the barista and the weather change. Detect and correct for variation such as a change of coffee lot, humidity or the state of the equipment, keeping deviation within the tolerance band.

The two purposes circle each other: maintenance is what lets you measure the effect of an improvement, and improvement is what raises the standard to be maintained. QC is the engine that turns this circle.

▸ In practice (three situations)

① Detecting anomalies against a baseline. Record a reference shot (dose, time, yield, taste) at opening every day, and when one day the shot runs fast and sour you can compare against the record and quickly find which of freshness, humidity or grinder wear has changed.

② Measuring improvement. When you introduce a new profile or recipe, only a baseline lets you compare whether it really is better. Maintenance is what makes improvement measurable, and improvement is what raises the standard to be maintained.

③ Responding to a change of lot. When the coffee lot changes, the same recipe tastes different. Compare against the reference shot, recalibrate grind and ratio, and update the baseline, and the variation the customer feels is minimised.

Sources Tier 1 KB quality_systems.md; ROASTING COURSE v2.pdf(Quality Control) Tier 2 SCA quality control practice

sections.title: What Do We Measure
sections.html:
10.2 · What To Measure

What Do We Measure

What cannot be measured cannot be managed. The object of QC is every variable that affects the reproducibility of extraction and roasting — in particular time, temperature, environment, measurement itself, and the consistency of the brewing method.

Objects of QC measurement
ObjectItems measuredWhy
TimeExtraction time · roast time · developmentDirect indicator of extraction yield and development
TemperatureWater temperature · roasting temperature · serving temperatureExtraction tone and the rate of roasting reactions
EnvironmentRoom temperature · humidity · bean temperatureAffects heat loss, grinding and degassing
Measurement ControlCalibration of scales, timers and refractometersThe reliability of the measuring tools themselves
Consistent Brewing MethodStandardisation of recipe and technique (SOP)The same result even when the person changes
Measure the measuring tools too

If the scale is 0.3g out or the refractometer is uncalibrated, every piece of data lies. This is why "Measurement Control" is included among the objects of QC — the reliability of the tools is the precondition of the reliability of the data.

▸ In practice (three situations)

① Finding patterns in environmental variables. When humidity↑ in the rainy season makes the coffee damp, grinding and flow rate change. Record environment (humidity) and time (extraction) and you discover that "the shot slows down at 75%+ humidity", and can build an SOP that coarsens the grind in advance.

② Calibrating the measuring tools themselves. If the scale is 0.3g out or the refractometer uncalibrated, all the data is false. Calibrating the tools regularly to secure the reliability of measurement is the precondition of QC.

③ Standardising the brewing method (SOP). Document the recipe and technique so that the same result comes out even when the person changes. Only once it is "the same cup whoever brews it" can maintenance and improvement be discussed. Measurement and standardisation are what make pre-emptive response possible.

Sources Tier 1 KB extraction_metrics.md · quality_systems.md; ROASTING COURSE v2.pdf Tier 2 SCA Brewing Control Chart; industry QC SOPs

sections.title: Priority — What to Control First
sections.html:
10.3 · Priority

Priority — What to Control First

You cannot control everything perfectly at once. QC too has an order of influence, of upstream first. Deviation upstream (roasting) carries further than deviation downstream (extraction).

◈ Why roasting comes first

Deviation in roasting is carried in every cup — if the batch swings, the result swings however well extraction is controlled. Upstream has to be locked down before downstream QC means anything. Stabilise in the order Roasting → Brewing.

◈ The hierarchy of sense and number

The outcome indicators take priority in the order Flavour → Texture → TDS (strength). A cup whose taste has collapsed is a failure even if TDS is within specification, so the numbers support the senses. Make the integrated judgement with Overall at the end.

A common misconception

"If TDS and extraction yield are within specification, it is good coffee" — false. TDS is an indicator of strength, not an indicator of quality. Average extraction yield can sit within range even when there is channelling. The numbers are the evidence for a sensory judgement and a tool for reproduction, not a substitute for taste.

▸ In practice (three situations)

① Lock down the upstream first. In the morning, approve the coffee with batch roast QC (colour, cupping), set the day's reference extraction, and then spot-check the cups that follow in the order Flavour → Texture → TDS. Upstream (roasting) has to be stabilised first for downstream QC to mean anything.

② Senses first, numbers in support. A cup whose taste has collapsed is a failure even if TDS is within specification. Under the hierarchy Flavour → Texture → TDS, use the numbers only as evidence for the sensory judgement and as a tool for reproduction. This avoids the misjudgement of "the yield is in range, so it is good".

③ Tracing back when a problem appears. When something goes wrong, walk the priority flow backwards to separate "is this roasting or extraction?" The priority order sets the route QC takes, so you do not cast about wondering where to look first.

Sources Tier 1 KB extraction_metrics.md · quality_systems.md · body_mouthfeel.md; ROASTING COURSE v2.pdf Tier 2 SCA Brewing Control Chart; SCA CVA

sections.title: Machine setup — minimum required heat
sections.html:
11.1 · Machine Setup

Machine setup — minimum required heat

Minimum Required Heat is the minimum heat application needed to roast a given batch size through without stalling. Where heat is insufficient, RoR stalls in the endothermic phase and the baked · dragging defects arise.

◈ Why it matters

Roasting demands a great deal of energy in the endothermic phase (moisture evaporation). If the heat application falls short of the batch size, the beans draw heat away, the rise in temperature stops, and the flavour turns flat (baked). In excess, the opposite: the surface scorches while the core stays under-developed.

◈ The relation to batch size

The larger the batch, the higher the heat capacity↑ → the greater the heat required↑, and the lower the RoR. Hence every machine has an appropriate batch range for its burner capacity. General guidance: charge about 60%–110% of drum capacity (in-house course material). Too little and the beans cannot hold on to the heat; too much and the heat runs short.

How to gauge the minimum heat

A working indicator: from a fully preheated state (drum, at least 30 minutes), if charging a normal batch still leaves RoR rising to 1st Crack without stalling or reversing, that is a sign the heat is sufficient. If instead RoR collapses in the middle of the roast, the batch must be reduced or more headroom in heat application is needed. Specific kcal/hour and burner capacity are [to verify] — refer to the equipment manual.

▸ In practice (three situations)

① Diagnosing an over-large batch. If a 5 kg drum charged with 4.5 kg gives a mid-roast RoR stall and a flat cup every time, the batch is too large for the available heat. Reduce the batch to 3–3.5 kg, or raise the preheat and the early heat application so that the endothermic phase is passed through without stalling.

② The problem of too small a batch. Conversely, charging less than 60% of drum capacity makes it easy for the beans to fail to hold on to the heat, so that the surface scorches while the core stays under-developed. Operate within 60–110% of drum capacity.

③ Zeroing the machine with preheat. The drum must be preheated thoroughly for at least 30 minutes for the heat to be stable from the first batch onwards. Where preheating is short, even the same profile wavers from batch to batch. A good profile too can only be drawn on top of sufficient heat and preheating.

Sources Tier 1 KB roast_curve.md · roasting_chemistry.md; ROASTING COURSE v2.pdf (Warming up · batch 60–110%) Tier 2 Rao The Coffee Roaster's Companion; equipment manuals Tier 3 [to verify: specific burner capacity]

sections.title: Environment setup — exhaust · electricity · gas · workflow
sections.html:
11.2 · Environment Setup

Environment setup — exhaust · electricity · gas · workflow

Roastery environment infrastructure checklist (conceptual frame)
ItemKey pointCaution
ExhaustDischarge of smoke · chaff · heat. Minimise flue diameter · length · bends; clean regularly (chaff = fire hazard)High exhaust resistance degrades airflow and roasting reproducibility. [to verify: local air-quality and fire codes]
ElectricityPower for motor · cooling · control gear. Stable capacity · dedicated circuit · earthingA momentary voltage drop damages RoR reproducibility. [to verify: rated capacity]
GasBurner fuel (LPG/LNG). Sufficient supply pressure · safety shut-offWhere supply pressure is short, heat application is insufficient and unstable. Installation by a licensed contractor is mandatory. [to verify: pipework specification]
WorkflowA one-way flow from green storage → charge → cooling → packingBack-flow and crossing paths bring contamination and inefficiency
Work EnvironmentRoom temperature · humidity · ventilation · noise · safety (extinguisher · CO alarm)High-temperature, dust-laden work — operator safety comes first
◈ Exhaust changes the roast

Exhaust is not mere ventilation. It bears directly on airflow within the drum (the share of convection · chaff removal), so that when the exhaust conditions change, the same profile gives a different result. Exhaust is therefore infrastructure and a roasting variable at once.

◈ Workflow makes quality and safety

When green coffee → roasting → cooling → packing flows in one direction, contamination, error and bottlenecks are reduced, and chaff and heat are separated from the working space, which makes it safe. A good workflow is the physical foundation of QC (Chapter 10).

▸ In practice (three situations)

① Settle the infrastructure first. In a new space, settle the exhaust (flue route · fire safety) and the gas and electrical capacity with a licensed professional first of all. Changing them later destroys roasting reproducibility, so setup comes before flavour tuning.

② Designing the workflow. Lay out green storage → charge → cooling → packing in one direction so that they do not overlap, reducing contamination and bottlenecks, and separate chaff and heat from the working space to secure safety.

③ Managing exhaust as a roasting variable. Exhaust is not mere ventilation but bears directly on airflow within the drum (convection · chaff removal). When flue resistance changes, the same profile gives a different result, so fix and record the exhaust conditions to protect reproducibility.

Sources Tier 1 KB roasting_chemistry.md; ROASTING COURSE v2.pdf (Type of Heats · Air Flow) Tier 2 Rao The Coffee Roaster's Companion Tier 3 local fire, air-quality and gas regulations [to verify]

sections.title: Evaluation · correction — minimum heat · 1st Crack development · energy
sections.html:
11.3 · Evaluation & Correction

Evaluation · correction — minimum heat · 1st Crack development · energy

◈ Calculating the minimum required heat (conceptual)

The principle is an energy balance: the energy needed to evaporate the moisture in the batch (latent heat) and to raise the beans to the target temperature ≥ the effective heat the burner actually delivers (efficiency taken into account). In practice it is verified by asking whether, with a normal batch, RoR rises through the endothermic phase without stalling. The exact kcal formula and the efficiency figure are [to verify: machine by machine].

◈ Correct development at 1st Crack

The temperature, RoR and timing at the moment of entry into 1st Crack govern the development that follows. Too early (excess energy) or too late (deficit) and the development goes astray. Adjust gas and airflow in advance so that RoR descends smoothly immediately after 1st Crack (avoiding a crash or a flick).

Energy Allocation — the end point of setup evaluation is, in the end, "on this machine and with this batch, how must energy be allocated along the time axis for the intended development to appear?" Generously in the endothermic phase, reduced in the exothermic. The setup (heat and exhaust) fixes the range of what is possible in this allocation, and profile design (Chapter 07) draws the curve within it.

Setup → profile → QC, one continuous line

This chapter (setup) builds the playing field on which the profile plays; Chapter 07 (profile) draws the curve upon it; and Chapter 10 (QC) reproduces that curve. The three chapters are one pipeline.

▸ In practice (three situations)

① Finding the minimum heat and the appropriate batch. On a new machine, test endothermic-phase RoR at several batch sizes to establish the minimum required heat at which it rises without stalling, and the appropriate batch range.

② Establishing a reference curve. With a representative coffee, record 1st Crack timing · RoR · drop temperature and build a reference curve. Only once this reference stands do profile design and QC thereafter run in the same language.

③ Verifying 1st Crack development. Check whether RoR descends smoothly immediately after 1st Crack (avoiding a crash or a flick), and where it does not, adjust gas and airflow in advance. Setup evaluation is the zeroing of all roasting.

Sources Tier 1 KB roast_curve.md · roasting_cracks.md · roasting_chemistry.md; ROASTING COURSE v2.pdf (Energy · 1st Crack) Tier 2 Rao The Coffee Roaster's Companion Tier 3 machine-by-machine thermal efficiency [to verify]

sections.title: Purpose — Why Compete
sections.html:
12.1 · Purpose

Purpose — Why Compete

◈ To represent the industry

The official purpose of the WBC is to select a person who can represent the whole of the specialty coffee industry. The champion speaks for the industry not only through technical skill but through their attitude to coffee, their communication and their vision.

◈ To train yourself and learn deeply

Preparing for a competition drives your own ability to its limit and makes you understand coffee far more deeply. The preparation process is itself the finest education available.

A competition is also a place where you connect with experts from other fields — farmers, green coffee traders, roasters, researchers and other baristas. That network determines both the quality of your preparation and the career that follows. The purposes are therefore four: representing the industry · personal development · deep learning · connection.

▸ In practice (three situations)

① Auditing your motivation for entering. If the only purpose is "the winner's trophy", preparation becomes unstable. Deciding which of the four purposes (representation, development, learning, connection) genuinely matters to you gives you the drive to keep preparing even through a slump.

② Turning preparation into a career asset. The knowledge of coffee, water and extraction and the network of farms and roasters built up through competition preparation remain regardless of whether you win. Feeding the preparation process into your own business or teaching content raises the return on the investment.

③ Growth at team level. When the baristas of a shop prepare for a competition together, capability in routine design, sensory and QC spreads to the whole team. The competition becomes both an individual's stage and the shop's training programme.

Sources Tier 1 KB wbc_2026_evaluation.md Tier 2 2026 WBC Official Rules & Regulations; World Coffee Championships

sections.title: Rules & Regulations — The First Priority · Breakdown · Analysis
sections.html:
12.2 · Rules & Regulations

Rules & Regulations — The First Priority · Breakdown · Analysis

The R&R (Rules & Regulations) is the constitution of the competition. Creativity is recognised only within it. Reading the rules precisely and turning them to your advantage is the first stage of preparation.

The First Priority

The first principle of preparation: do what the scoresheet rewards. However fine an idea may be, it earns no points if it is not connected to a scoring item. Read the R&R and the scoresheet first, then reverse-engineer the routine from them.

R&R Breakdown

WBC round structure (2026)
RoundCompetitorsTimeBeverages
Round OneAll15 min4 espresso + 4 milk + 4 signature = 12 servings (Technical Judge in attendance)
Semi-FinalTop 15 + 1 Wild Card15 min12 servings (no Technical Judge)
FinalTop 615 min12 servings

Core definitions (→ expanded in Chapter 03): Espresso is approximately 30 mL, drawn as a single continuous extraction (90.5–96℃, 8.5–9.5 bar, 3.0 s deviation across the four cups, crema mandatory). Milk is at least one shot plus steamed milk (plant-based permitted, additives prohibited). Signature must incorporate at least four shots, be prepared on stage, and contains no alcohol or controlled substances. The rules on Team Bar attendance and the Wild Card are also found in this section.

R&R Analysis

The broken-down rules are then converted into opportunities: where is there latitude (for example, the creativity of the signature beverage, or freedom of temperature), and where are the absolute prohibitions (alcohol, additives, time overrun)? Eliminate the absolute prohibitions at source through rehearsal, and concentrate differentiation on the items with the greatest latitude.

A common misconception

"The WBC requires a 1:2 ratio or a specific recipe" — false (no ratio is specified). "Alcohol is allowed in the signature beverage" — false (it is prohibited). Knowing the rules precisely avoids both unnecessary self-censorship and fatal disqualification.

▸ In practice (three situations)

① Concentrate differentiation where there is latitude. Pour your originality into the space the rules leave open, such as the creativity of the signature beverage and freedom of temperature. Trying to stand out where the rules are fixed (the definition of espresso) invites nothing but deductions and disqualification.

② Block the prohibitions through rehearsal. With absolute prohibitions such as alcohol, additives and time overrun, a single mistake means zero for the category. Put them on the rehearsal checklist so that they are internalised and never crossed on stage.

③ Re-confirm the current rules. Since the R&R is revised every year, using last year's routine unchanged may fall foul of an altered clause. Read the official R&R for that year again from the beginning and mark every change.

Sources Tier 1 KB competition_round_format.md · wbc_espresso_definition.md · wbc_milk_beverage.md · wbc_signature_beverage.md Tier 2 2026 WBC Official Rules & Regulations §2–3

sections.title: Scoresheet — Sensory · Technical · Head Judge
sections.html:
12.3 · Scoresheet

Scoresheet — Sensory · Technical · Head Judge

The scoresheet is the blueprint of the routine. Once you know the scale and the weighting of each item, it is settled where you should invest your time and care.

Essentials of the WBC Sensory Scoresheet (identical for all 4 Sensory Judges)
PartMain itemsScale (weighting)
I. EspressoCrema / Taste·Tactile Accuracy / Taste·Tactile ExperienceYes-No, 0–3(×2), 0–6(×4·×2)
II. MilkVisual Appeal / Taste Accuracy / Taste Experience0–3, 0–3(×2), 0–6(×4)
III. SignatureTaste Accuracy / Well explained / Taste Experience0–3(×2), 0–6(×2), 0–6(×4)
IV. BaristaAttention to detail / Presentation / Coffee knowledge and use of equipment0–3, 0–6(×2)
V. Total ImpressionOverall impression0–6(×2)
◈ Technical Scoresheet (Round One)

Clean cloths (at least 3) · group head flush · dry basket · permitted spillage and waste (≤5 g per category, excellent ≤1 g) · consistent dosing · tamping · 3.0 s deviation in extraction time · portafilter cleanliness · immediate extraction · station management. Technical hygiene and accuracy are scored Yes/No and 0–3.

◈ Head Judge's

Coordinates and oversees the Sensory and Technical judgements, approves the awarding of a zero, and in the Semi-final and Final absorbs the items left by the absent Technical Judge (station management and clean-down). The final guarantor of consistency.

Read the weightings

Taste Experience carries ×4, the heaviest weighting of all. In other words, "the pleasure of the flavour" carries the highest allocation of points. Rather than a spectacular performance, the core of the score is a cup that is genuinely delicious, whose descriptors are precise (Accuracy) and whose experience is enjoyable (Experience).

▸ In practice (three situations)

① Building the script from the scoresheet. For every item, mark "where does this become points". In the signature explanation (Well explained ×2), convey the ingredients and flavours factually and announce in advance, with precision, the descriptors the judges will perceive, thereby securing Accuracy.

② Allocate time by weighting. Since Taste Experience (×4) carries the highest allocation, pour your preparation time into a genuinely delicious cup rather than a spectacular performance. Do not over-invest in elements with low allocations.

③ Train Accuracy and Experience separately. "Are the descriptors accurate (Accuracy)" and "is the experience enjoyable (Experience)" are two different matters. In rehearsal, take feedback on the two axes separately and practise repeatedly until the flavour you announced and the flavour actually delivered coincide.

Sources Tier 1 KB wbc_2026_evaluation.md · scoring_scales.md Tier 2 2024 WBC Sensory/Technical/Head Judge Scoresheet (in-house materials); 2026 WBC R&R §13–15

sections.title: System — The Evaluation System · Competition Operations
sections.html:
12.4 · System

System — The Evaluation System · Competition Operations

◈ Evaluation System

4 Sensory Judges + (in Round One) 1 Technical Judge + 1 Head Judge. Five scales (Yes/No · 0–3 Accuracy · 0–3 Impression · 0–6 Experience · CVA 0–9) are multiplied by their weightings and totalled. A zero always requires Head Judge approval. Scores do not carry over between rounds.

◈ Competition Operations

15 minutes of competition time (plus set-up and clean-down), time overrun penalties, Team Bar and Wild Card, tie-breaking (Espresso > Milk > Total Impression). Rules on the station, equipment and bringing in green coffee. Knowing the operational rules is what avoids unnecessary deductions.

▸ In practice (three situations)

① Turning the tie-break rule to your advantage. Knowing the tie-break order (Espresso > Milk > Total Impression) establishes a strategy of putting particular effort into the espresso course. The rule tells you the priority.

② Designing the timeline. To produce 12 servings in 15 minutes without deviation, design the movement and timing to the second, and internalise the time overrun penalty and the waste rule (≤5 g) through rehearsal.

③ Preparing for the character of each round. A Technical Judge is in attendance in Round One, so hygiene and technical accuracy matter there; in the Semi-final and Final the Technical Judge is absent, so allow for the items the Head Judge absorbs and adjust the intensity of preparation round by round.

Sources Tier 1 KB wbc_2026_evaluation.md · competition_round_format.md · scoring_scales.md · tie_breaker_rules.md Tier 2 2026 WBC R&R §2, §10, §13

sections.title: Intensive Research — What to Dig Into, and How
sections.html:
12.5 · Intensive Research

Intensive Research — What to Dig Into, and How

A winning routine stands on extensive research. The heart of this section is not blind practice but systematising what it is you should investigate.

WBC intensive research areas
AreaWhat to investigate
Past finalistsFinal presentations of the last five years plus the historic great performances — dissect the structure, the concept and the mode of delivery. [to verify: confirm each year's results and videos through the official channels]
CoffeeCountry, processing, variety, flavour profile, recipe — the narrative of why this coffee
TechnicThe latest techniques in extraction, distribution, tamping and use of the machine
EquipmentGrinder, machine, water, tools — the optimal combination within the rules
ThemeThe message and narrative running through the whole stage
Signature DrinksThe ideas, structures and success or failure factors of past signature beverages
Research is the search for the "why"

Good study of a finalist looks not at "what did they do" but at "why did that become points". Tracing back which item of the scoresheet the coffee selection, the technique and the signature beverage were aimed at leaves you with the principle you can transplant into your own routine.

▸ In practice (three situations)

① Reverse-engineering the finalists. Break down the final videos of the last five years into structure (opening – development – close), concept, coffee and signature beverage, and trace back which scoresheet item each choice was aimed at. Extract the principle, not the imitation.

② Coffee sourcing research. Narrow down "which country, processing and variety suit this concept" on the basis of the flavour profile, then approach green coffee traders and farms to secure a small high-quality lot for the competition. The coffee becomes the physical evidence of the concept.

③ Keeping equipment and technique current. Investigate the latest developments in grinders, machines and techniques and find the optimal combination within the rules. Note, however, that newest is not automatically best — select on whether it contributes to your concept and your coffee.

Sources Tier 1 KB wbc_2026_evaluation.md · varieties.md · origin_terroir.md Tier 2 World Coffee Championships official archive Tier 3 Final videos and interviews for each year [to verify]

sections.title: Concept — From Research to a Single Message
sections.html:
12.6 · Concept

Concept — From Research to a Single Message

A concept is the single core message running through the whole stage. When the coffee, the technique, the signature beverage and the spoken lines all point towards that message, the routine acquires persuasive force.

◈ Research → Interests

Find in your research the point that genuinely interests you. A concept without authenticity shows on stage. "Why am I sincere about this coffee, this subject" is the seed of the concept.

◈ Concept Development

Compress that interest into a single sentence, then develop it consistently through the coffee selection, the signature beverage, the technique and the spoken lines. Every element should prove the concept.

▸ In practice (three situations)

① Aligning everything to one message. If the concept is "a new sweetness created by this farm's processing innovation", then align accordingly — the coffee is that farm's experimental lot, the signature beverage uses ingredients that amplify sweetness, the spoken lines cover the relationship and the processing, and the technique is a recipe for maximum extraction of sweetness.

② Auditing authenticity. If "why am I sincere about this subject" is weak, it shows on stage. Only by taking the point that genuinely interested you during research as the seed of the concept will your lines and your expression carry conviction.

③ Proving it through flavour. When the judges confirm the concept in the cup, Accuracy and Experience rise together. A concept that exists only in words and not in the flavour earns no points — design every element so that it proves the concept through flavour.

Sources Tier 1 KB wbc_signature_beverage.md · wbc_2026_evaluation.md Tier 2 WBC finalist presentation methodology (official archive)

sections.title: Routine and Presentation Development
sections.html:
12.7 · Routine / Presentation Development

Routine and Presentation Development

This is the stage of realising the concept as 15 minutes of live performance. From idea to stage, completeness is built up in a set order.

  1. Theme & Concept — fix the single message (12.6).
  2. Mind Mapping — generate the ideas that branch out from the concept.
  3. Key Factors — compare against the scoresheet and select the decisive battlegrounds (divergence → convergence).
  4. Coffee — settle on a coffee that satisfies both the concept and the score.
  5. Signature Drink Ideas — design a signature beverage that proves the concept through flavour (in compliance with the rules: four shots, no alcohol).
  6. Draft Speech & Routine — a first draft of the lines, the movement and the timeline. Map lines and actions to every scoring item.
  7. Technical Training — repeated training to produce 12 servings without deviation and within the time.
  8. Fine-Tuning — refine the lines, the recipe and the movement through rehearsal and feedback to reach completion.
Diverge → converge → repeat

The early phase (mind mapping) is broad divergence, the middle phase (Key Factors) is dispassionate convergence against the scoresheet, and the late phase (training and fine-tuning) is stabilisation through repetition. It is the balance between creativity and the realities of scoring that makes a winning routine.

▸ In practice (three situations)

① Mapping the score onto the lines. Write the targeted scoring item beside each sentence: "explanation of processing (→ Coffee Knowledge)", "you will perceive grapefruit and honey (→ Taste Accuracy, announced in advance)". Inscribe the concept (feeling) and the score (reality) into the same script.

② Diverge → converge → repeat. Diverge broadly with mind mapping, converge dispassionately against the scoresheet at Key Factors, then stabilise through repetition with Technical Training and fine-tuning. It is the balance between creativity and the realities of scoring that makes a winning routine.

③ Measured technical training. Train with measurement so that the 12 servings are produced repeatedly within a 3.0 s extraction deviation and the waste rule (≤5 g). Stability must be secured by numbers, not by feel, if you are not to falter on stage.

Sources Tier 1 KB wbc_2026_evaluation.md · wbc_signature_beverage.md · scoring_scales.md Tier 2 2026 WBC R&R; WBC finalist preparation methodology (official archive) Tier 3 Chanho Hong's competition preparation experience (winner, 2018 Australian Central Region Brewers Cup)

sections.title: Purpose — why the Brewers Cup
sections.html:
13.1 · Purpose

Purpose — why the Brewers Cup

◈ Representing the industry · self-development

The same broad purpose as the WBC — to select someone to represent the industry, and through the preparation to train and deepen oneself. The focus, however, is placed on the essence of brewing.

◈ Deep study · connection

Brewing reveals the interaction of green coffee, water and extraction in its purest form. In preparing, one digs deep into water chemistry and extraction theory and becomes connected to producers and researchers.

The appeal of the WBrC lies in making "the most refined difference out of the simplest coffee". In place of the spectacle of espresso, the language of the stage is the transparent completeness of a single cup.

▸ In practice (three situations)

① A reason to go deeper into water and extraction theory. Preparing for the WBrC forces you into water chemistry and extraction theory. The knowledge gained in that process raises the level of the shop's brewing and QC wholesale after the competition.

② A network of producers and researchers. Searching out rare lots and designing water connects you with farms, green coffee traders and researchers. Those relationships become an asset for later sourcing and collaboration.

③ Establishing a brewing identity. Preparation that concentrates on "a simple cup of filter" becomes the occasion for refining your own extraction philosophy and signature method. The competition is itself a training ground for personal branding.

Sources Tier 1 KB wbrc_2025_evaluation.md Tier 2 2025 World Brewers Cup Rules & Regulations

sections.title: Rules & Regulations — the first priority · breakdown · analysis
sections.html:
13.2 · Rules & Regulations

Rules & Regulations — the first priority · breakdown · analysis

The First Priority

The same as the WBC: do what the scoresheet rewards. The WBrC, however, has two services of different character — the Open Service (your own coffee, free choice) and the Compulsory Service (coffee provided by the competition) — and each demands a different strategy.

R&R Breakdown — round structure

WBrC round structure (2025; varies with the number of competitors)
CaseRound structure
≤ 38 competitors (3 rounds)Round One(Open) → Semi-Final(Compulsory) → Final(Open)
> 38 competitors (2 rounds)Round One(Open) → Final(Open + Compulsory)
  • Open Service — your own coffee, 3 cups of the same beverage → judged by 3 judges. 5 min set-up + 10 min performance time. (Disqualification beyond 11 min; beyond 10:00, −0.5 points per second, up to −30)
  • Compulsory Service — brewed with the 350 g of coffee provided by the competition, and includes assessment of Sensory Uniformity. Since the information cannot be known in advance, it tests on-the-spot judgement.

R&R Analysis — analysis

The weapon in the Open is optimisation in advance (coffee · water · recipe · narrative); the weapon in the Compulsory is cupping on the spot and deciding a recipe quickly. Analyse the difference in point allocation and character between the two services and design the preparation separately. The round structure is confirmed 8 weeks before the competition.

A common misconception

"The Brewers Cup also serves 12 cups" — false (3 cups). "The WBrC is assessed on 10 attributes" — false (7 Cup attributes + 4 Barista attributes). Only by knowing the structure precisely does the preparation stay on course.

▸ In practice (three situations)

① Dual preparation for Open and Compulsory. The Open targets the limit of optimisation in advance (coffee · water · recipe · narrative); the Compulsory targets cupping and recipe decisions on the spot. Because their character differs, split the practice into two designs.

② Internalise the time regulations. Learn the 10 min performance time, disqualification beyond 11 min and the overrun deductions as a second-by-second timeline in the body. Rehearse so that the three-cup service and the explanation finish within the time.

③ Confirm the round format. The round structure changes with the number of competitors (≤ 38 vs > 38) and is confirmed 8 weeks beforehand, so as soon as it is confirmed, redistribute the weighting between Open and Compulsory preparation.

◈ Head Judge's Scoresheet

In the Open, Overall Workflow and Technical Uniformity (consistency of ratio, grind, brewer, filter, time, temperature and turbulence across the 3 cups) are assessed at 0–3 × 4. In the Compulsory, the Head Judge looks at Sensory Uniformity and the Beverage Information Form. The consistency of the 3 cups is the Head Judge's central concern.

◈ Maximum score · time

Open Service maximum 226 points, Compulsory maximum 213 points. Performance time 10 min, disqualification at 11 min. Time and consistency are the major deduction risks and therefore the points to manage.

Intensity ≠ quality (again)

All 7 attributes use a 0–9 intensity scale, but a higher intensity does not mean a higher score. The intensity of Acidity and Mouthfeel is unrelated to quality — the judging looks at how well that intensity works (→ Chapter 03). Tie-break: Flavor > Aftertaste > Overall.

▸ In practice (three situations)

① Choosing the coffee by the tie-break rule. Knowing the tie-break (Flavor > Aftertaste > Overall), you invest in a coffee and a recipe with outstanding density of Flavor and Aftertaste. The rule gives you the criterion for selection.

② Securing uniformity across the 3 cups. For Technical Uniformity, standardise weighing, timing and turbulence to the second. Since the Head Judge looks at the consistency of the 3 cups, it is not one cup but three cups that must be the same.

③ Announcing the descriptors. In the script, announce precisely the flavours the judges will perceive, and so secure Accuracy. The key is to show not the intensity but "how well that intensity works" (intensity ≠ quality).

13.4 · System

System — evaluation system · competition operations

◈ Evaluation System

3 Sensory judges + 1 Head Judge. The 7 Cup attributes (0–9) measure the result, while the Barista Evaluation measures process and communication separately. The Compulsory additionally looks at Uniformity and the accuracy of the information. Scores of 0–3 require Head Judge approval.

◈ Competition Operation

Open: 5 min set-up + 10 min performance; 3 cups of the same beverage. Regulations on time overrun and waste, and on the water and equipment brought in. Since the number of rounds changes with the number of competitors, check the competition format in advance.

▸ In practice (three situations)

① Time management in the Open. To finish set-up, explanation and 3 cups consistently within 10 min, fix water temperature, weighing and timing with advance set-up and a checklist. Internalise disqualification beyond 11 min and the overrun deductions through rehearsal.

② Preparing for the Compulsory. Repeat the training of grasping an unknown coffee in a 5-minute cupping and deciding the recipe. Its character differs from the advance optimisation of the Open, so on-the-spot judgement has to be built separately.

③ Confirm the round format. The number of rounds (3 vs 2) changes with the number of competitors and is confirmed 8 weeks before the competition, so check the format in advance and allocate the weighting between Open and Compulsory preparation.

13.5 · Intensive Research

Intensive research — coffee · water · technique

WBrC research resembles that for the WBC, but one axis is decisively added: water. The difference in a single cup of filter is largely decided by the composition of the water.

WBrC intensive research areas
AreaWhat
Past finalistsThe structure, coffee, recipe and delivery of the last 5 years plus the great presentations of the past. [to verify: confirm results and videos through official channels]
CoffeeCountry · processing · variety · flavour · recipe — rarity and narrative
TechnicDripper · pour pattern · flow rate · turbulence · interval design (→ Chapter 04)
EquipmentThe combination of dripper · grinder · kettle · filter
WaterCa · Mg · alkalinity custom water design — controlling the direction of acidity, sweetness and body (→ Chapter 02)
ThemeThe message that runs through the stage
Water is where it is won

The top competitors at the WBrC design their custom water with precision. Empirically, raising the proportion of magnesium is associated with the complexity and acidity side, raising the proportion of calcium with the sweetness and body side, and lowering alkalinity with preserving acidity. The same coffee becomes a different cup through water, so water is an independent axis of the research (→ Chapter 02.3). ※ The directionality of Mg/Ca is an empirical tendency, and the binding of specific acids is not academically established, so always verify blind to confirm the actual difference.

▸ In practice (three situations)

① Designing direction through water. For "brighter", test water with a raised proportion of magnesium; for "rounder", water with a raised proportion of calcium. But do not lean on the tendency — settle it with A/B blind scoring using the same coffee and the same recipe.

② Three-way coherence of coffee, water and recipe. For a high-grown, acidity-driven coffee, match low-alkalinity water that keeps the acidity alive with a bright extraction; for a sweetness-driven coffee, water that supports the body with a stable extraction. Align the three axes on a single objective.

③ Linking technique and equipment research. Investigate drippers (cone, flat bottom, hybrid), pour patterns and flow rate together with the water design, and narrow down by experiment the combination that creates the flavour you want. It is not water alone but the whole extraction that decides the result.

sections.title: Concept — the message carried in one cup
sections.html:
13.6 · Concept

Concept — the message carried in one cup

◈ Research → Interests → Development

The same flow as the WBC — find genuine interest in the research, compress the concept into a single sentence, and develop it through coffee, water, recipe and script. Since the only medium is a single cup of filter, however, the connection between concept and taste has to be more direct.

◈ Why it has to be purer

There is no screen such as milk or a signature drink. The concept must be proved immediately by the coffee selection, the water and the extraction. It persuades only when "why this coffee, why this water, why this recipe" runs in a straight line from the concept.

▸ In practice (three situations)

① A straight line from coffee to water to recipe. If the concept is "the crystallisation of acidity made by altitude" — choose a high-grown washed coffee, emphasise acidity and complexity by raising magnesium in the water (this being an empirical tendency, verify it blind), and set the recipe at a temperature and ratio that keep the acidic range alive.

② Using the purity of filter. Since there is no screen such as milk or a signature drink, "why this coffee, this water, this recipe" must connect directly to the concept. The script ties altitude, variety and water design into a single story.

③ Proving it in the taste. Points come when the judges taste the concept in the cup. The link between concept and taste has to be more direct than in the WBC for it to persuade — the single cup is itself the presentation.

13.7 · Routine / Presentation Development

Routine · presentation development

The concept is realised as one cup in ten minutes. The flow of diverge → converge → repeat is the same as in the WBC, but what matters here is the three-way coherence of coffee, water and extraction and the perfect consistency of the 3 cups.

  1. Theme & Concept — fix the one-sentence message (13.6).
  2. Mind Mapping — diverge across the possibilities of coffee, water, technique and narrative.
  3. Key Factors — check against the scoresheet (Flavor and Aftertaste first) and select where the result will be decided.
  4. Coffee — fix the coffee that satisfies both the concept and the score.
  5. Draft Speech & Routine — draft the script, movement and timeline, mapping the score item targeted to each line.
  6. Technical Training — repetition until the 3 cups are brewed without deviation (standardising weighing, temperature and turbulence). For the Compulsory, training in deciding a recipe on the spot.
  7. Fine-Tuning — refine water, recipe and script through rehearsal and feedback until complete.
Dual preparation: Open vs Compulsory

For the Open, prepare the limit of optimisation in advance (coffee · water · recipe · narrative); for the Compulsory, build separately the training of grasping and adjusting to an unfamiliar coffee quickly. The two preparations differ in character, so the practice methods must be split as well.

▸ In practice (three situations)

① Aligning the Open script with the score. Match the announcement to the score — "you will find grapefruit, black tea and a long finish (→ Flavor · Aftertaste Accuracy)" — and repeat while measuring the ratio, temperature and turbulence of the 3 cups.

② Compulsory loop training. Every week, run the loop of 5-minute cupping of an unknown coffee → fixing the recipe → reproducing 3 cups to build on-the-spot judgement and reproducibility. Keep the practice method separate from the Open.

③ Verifying the custom water. Make the water for the Open in several compositions, confirm the actual difference by blind scoring on the seven attributes, and only then fix it. Do not take "Mg is brighter" on faith — harden it with data. The preparation is itself the stability on stage.
